qAndA.answer: Robert Malley states that there is a humanitarian crisis going on in Yemen. With the United Nations reporting it as the worst they have seen.
qAndA.question: What is happening in Yemen according to Robert Malley?

qAndA.answer: Because it is the worst humanitarian crisis in the world, with a child dying every 12 minutes due to conflict.
qAndA.question: Why does Robert Malley say the world should care about Yemen?

qAndA.answer: Robert Malley believes that if people make the right decisions, the conflict can be resolved.
qAndA.question: What does Robert Malley think can end the conflict in Yemen?

qAndA.answer: Malley claims that the Crisis Group's work on the ground for over a decade has resulted in their team building relationships of trust and confidence with all actors in the conflict.
qAndA.question: What does Robert Malley say is the product of the Crisis Group's work?

qAndA.answer: Robert Malley says that the actors in the Yemen conflict respect the Crisis Group's work and view them as a trustworthy source of information and advice.
qAndA.question: How do actors involved in the Yemen conflict view the Crisis Group?

text_to_speech: There's a simple reason why the world should care about Yemen. It's the worst humanitarian crisis that it faces today, according to the United Nations, you have a child dying because of conflict every 12 minutes, you have levels of malnutrition, hunger, starvation, and cholera that are rivaling anything we're seeing anywhere else in the world. And it's a conflict that can be ended, if people take the right decisions. As with most conflicts, there's a complex number of reasons why it began, why it's continuing, why it's not ending. Local grievances that go back a very long time, regional players that are using proxies on the ground, to advance their own interests and global powers that are either indifferent or they're seeing a benefit in perpetuating the conflict. So at some level, you're going to have to address all three. But there also are some clear decisions that only a few number of actors can make, and that's what Crisis Group has been insisting upon from the outset. Outside actors, rather than fueling the conflict, can take very concrete steps to de-escalate the war, and bring the parties back to the negotiating table. What I saw when I was in Aden, and which is really the product of Crisis Group’s work on the ground for over a decade now, is that our team has built relations of trust and confidence, with all actors, all competing actors on the ground. And that's not just true at the local level, because with our team, we then travelled to Saudi Arabia, where we met with senior Saudi leaders. We went to other countries in the region where we met with leaders of the Huthi movement. We've spoken to Iranian leaders. And each one of them has told us that they want to hear our views. They respect what we have to say, they think that it's a fair rendition of a very polarised situation, and they want to hear our advice and recommendations One thing that struck me, particularly in Aden, but also in other parts of the region, is how the actors that Crisis Group has been talking to now since 2009, or earlier in some cases, about Yemen. Number one, they respect the fact that we're not late comers who just come there, because the country is aflame, they know that our team cares about Yemen, has taken time to meet with a wide array of actors there. And they tell us: “I remember your report, you were the first who spoke about the southerners and a southerner who says we don't particularly agree with what you're saying now, but we know it comes from the right place because you wrote about us and you represented our views fairly a decade ago”. We meet with the Huthis they say: “you know, you're being unfair on some issues, but we remember you came speak to us at a time when nobody wanted to talk to us”. The same with the Hadi government, same with other countries, regional countries. And it's that deep connection that has been established, in the case of Yemen, for a decade, that has helped us establish ourselves as an institution that people look to, for the answer to their question, which is: What's happening? What can we do about it? What is the solution that's out there that we haven't found yet?

youtube_description: Robert Malley, Crisis Group's President and CEO, discusses the conflict in Yemen - why it began and why it is still ongoing -, and reflects on the relationships Crisis Group has built with all actors involved.
youtube_title: Robert Malley on Crisis Group's Mission in Yemen
